enrichment.short_title: Arsenal trade marks and badge-of-allegiance use
key_facts: Matthew Reed sold unofficial Arsenal football merchandise bearing registered Arsenal signs identical to Arsenal's class 25 marks.
Laddie J referred questions to the ECJ (Case C-206/01) on whether non-origin-indicating 'badge of allegiance' use could infringe; the ECJ ruled Arsenal should succeed.
On remittal the judge treated the ECJ as having exceeded its jurisdiction on facts and dismissed the infringement claim.
The Court of Appeal held the ECJ judgment addressed whether use jeopardised the guarantee-of-origin function, not whether use was 'trade mark use' in a narrow sense.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Laddie J's second judgment following an ECJ reference on trade mark infringement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judgment for Arsenal on registered trade mark infringement.
enrichment.ratio: Under Article 5(1)(a) of the Trade Marks Directive and section 10(1) of the Trade Marks Act 1994, identical sign use on identical goods infringes if it affects or is liable to affect the registered mark's functions, especially its essential guarantee-of-origin function; it is immaterial that consumers may perceive the sign as a badge of support or loyalty, and a national court must follow the ECJ's ruling on interpretation even where the operative wording refers to the circumstances of the case.
legal_issues: Whether identical-sign use must indicate trade origin to infringe under section 10(1)
Whether the ECJ exceeded its jurisdiction by making findings inconsistent with the trial judge
Whether Mr Reed's use was liable to jeopardise Arsenal's guarantee of origin
Whether the ECJ ruling was binding on the national court
linked_authorities: Arsenal Football Club Plc v Reed (Case C-206/01)
British Sugar Plc v James Robertson & Sons Ltd
Phillips Electronics NV v Remington Consumer Products Ltd
Lloyd Schuhfabrik Meyer & Co GmbH v Klysen Handel BV
R v Secretary of State for Transport ex parte Factortame (No 5)
Vine Products Ltd v Mackenzie & Co Ltd

confidence.notes: Outcome, ratio, ECJ interaction, and statutory framework are explicit; passing-off reasoning obiter only.

enrichment.short_title: Listed building enforcement against predecessor works

statutes_considered.title: Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990

key_facts: Mr Braun bought listed St Paul's Studios in 2000 and carried out internal alterations without listed building consent.
Hammersmith and Fulham served a listed building enforcement notice and prosecuted him; he appealed on grounds including that requirements exceeded reversal of his own works.
Ouseley J allowed Braun's appeals and remitted the enforcement decision; the Secretary of State appealed on the scope of enforcement powers.
The enforcement notice alleged contraventions in terms focused on Braun's works, used 'original' ambiguously, and the Council deleted items it accepted he had not done.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State appeal from Ouseley J's decision allowing statutory challenges to an inspector's dismissal of a section 39 enforcement notice appeal and refusal of listed building consent.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; inspector's decision on the enforcement notice remained quashed and the matter remitted to the Secretary of State.
enrichment.ratio: A local planning authority may enforce by listed building enforcement notice against the present owner in respect of any unauthorised works since listing, including works by predecessors, but section 38(2) requires the notice to specify the alleged contravention with sufficient clarity; where, as here, the notice was apt only to reverse Braun's own works, the inspector could not lawfully treat it as requiring restoration to the 1970 listed condition.
legal_issues: Whether enforcement may reach contravening works by predecessors since listing
Whether the enforcement notice sufficiently specified the works to be reversed
Whether restoration requirements must relate only to the owner's own alterations
Whether the inspector erred on the section 20 consent appeal
linked_authorities: Bath City Council v Secretary of State for the Environment

confidence.notes: Two-issue structure and outcome are clear; partial disagreement with Ouseley J on the section 20 appeal is noted but does not affect the main ratio.

enrichment.short_title: Bankruptcy where petition debt fully secured

statutes_considered.title: Trusts of Land and Appointment of Trustees Act 1996

key_facts: Barclays obtained a bankruptcy order against Mr Owo-Samson based on a partly secured costs debt, estimating security at £20,000 on a forced-sale valuation of £145,000.
Owo-Samson did not challenge the security valuation at the petition hearing but later sought annulment under section 282 with retrospective evidence valuing the home at £210,000 in June 1998.
The Registrar refused annulment, treating enforcement-cost assumptions and the debtor's resistance to sale as relevant; Judge McGonigal dismissed the appeal.
Chadwick LJ granted a second appeal on whether section 269(1)(b) displaced the section 271(1)(a) secured-debt inquiry.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from refusal to annul a bankruptcy order made on a creditor's petition.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; annulment application remitted to a different registrar for redetermination on the correct legal basis.
enrichment.ratio: A creditor's statement of estimated security under section 269(1)(b) does not prevent the court at the petition or annulment stage from determining whether the petition debt was fully secured when properly valued; projected costs of opposed enforcement should not be deducted in that exercise, and discretion to annul must be exercised without treating irrelevant factors such as TOLATA section 15 principles or the debtor's expected obstruction of sale as defeating a finding of full security.
legal_issues: Effect of a section 269 security estimate on section 271(1)(a)
Whether annulment under section 282(1)(a) is available where the debt was fully secured
Whether enforcement costs form part of the secured debt for bankruptcy purposes
Exercise of discretion to annul after delay and changed valuation evidence
linked_authorities: Platts v Western Trust & Savings Ltd
Royal Bank of Scotland v Farley

confidence.notes: Core statutory analysis and remittal outcome are explicit; discretion on rehearing remains fact-sensitive.

enrichment.short_title: Interim care order without welfare analysis
key_facts: A Hasidic family with six minor children faced public law proceedings after a therapist disclosed alleged historic sexual abuse by a grandfather and concerns about the mother's conduct.
Dr Lindsey provided a limited court statement confirming abuse disclosures but not full strategy-meeting detail; the local authority moved from wardship to Children Act proceedings.
Sumner J made interim care orders on 1-2 May 2003 despite the authority conceding removal was unnecessary to interview the children.
Hackney issued the care application late in the Principal Registry, so no children's guardian was initially appointed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent appeal with permission granted at the outset against interim care orders made at a contested hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; interim care orders set aside and the application adjourned with liberty to apply on short notice; a guardian appointed.
enrichment.ratio: Although the section 31 threshold may be crossed on a broad assessment of Dr Lindsey's evidence and surrounding material, a judge may not make an interim care order without conducting the separate welfare and proportionality exercise required by Article 8, including consideration of less radical alternatives; where removal is not necessary, adjourning with liberty on the authority to apply is ordinarily preferable to a conditional interim care order placing the burden on parents to veto removal.
legal_issues: Whether there was sufficient evidence to cross the section 31 threshold
Whether Dr Lindsey's evidence was adequately challengeable
Whether an interim care order was necessary and proportionate
Procedural defects arising from late issue of the care application

confidence.notes: Court accepted threshold crossed but unanimously faulted the order made; outcome and two-stage analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Planning fallback and section 73 time extension
key_facts: Mr Cox sought planning permission for a dwelling at Woodlands, Ponsanooth, in countryside and an area of great landscape value; Carrick refused and an inspector dismissed his appeal.
He relied on a fallback to implement an earlier approved scheme, arguing a 1996 application had renewed time under the 1992 outline permission.
The Council treated the confused 1996 application as a fresh section 73 permission with new reserved-matter and commencement deadlines; Cox missed the 1999 reserved-matters deadline.
Cox also argued legitimate expectation based on informal officer advice and misleading council communications.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash an inspector's decision dismissing a planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; inspector's refusal of planning permission upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A muddled application seeking further time may lawfully be determined as a fresh planning permission under section 73 rather than a renewal under Regulation 3(3)(a), starting new condition deadlines; where reserved matters under the 1996 permission were not approved in time there was no extant fallback, and mistaken informal advice did not create a legitimate expectation sufficient to outweigh strong development-plan objections.
legal_issues: Whether the 1996 application was a renewal or a section 73 permission
Whether an approved reserved-matters decision from 1994 carried forward to the 1996 permission
Whether a fallback development right remained available at appeal
Whether council misadvice gave rise to legitimate expectation or estoppel
linked_authorities: Henry Boot Homes Ltd v Bassetlaw District Council
R v Leicestershire County Council ex parte Powergen

confidence.notes: Planning history and inspector's fallback analysis are detailed; costs discussion omitted from ratio.

notes: Batch 86 enrichment; 2-1 split (Wilson and Brooke LJ; Hale LJ dissenting)

enrichment.short_title: Benefits recovery and business rent award
key_facts: Mrs Chatwin, a self-employed insurance broker, closed her loss-making business after a road accident and remained liable for rent under her office lease until May 1998.
She abandoned a conventional loss-of-earnings claim because the business generated no net profit, but recovered 5/7 of a rent settlement as damage from destruction of the business.
The county court judge and Cox J refused to characterise that award as 'compensation for earnings lost' under Schedule 2 for benefit-recoupment purposes.
A certificate of recoverable benefits included £12,249.08 severe disablement allowance over a longer period than the earnings-related award.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal on the meaning of Schedule 2, column 1, item 1 of the Social Security (Recovery of Benefits) Act 1997.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed by majority (Wilson and Brooke LJ; Hale LJ dissenting); rent-related award held to be compensation for earnings lost.
enrichment.ratio: On the majority view, 'compensation for earnings lost' in Schedule 2 includes an award compensating business receipts that would have met ongoing professional expenses such as rent, not merely net profit; where a self-employed claimant loses turnover used to discharge liabilities continuing after closure, that award falls within the earnings head and is subject to deduction of equivalent income-replacement benefits, even though conventional personal injury loss-of-earnings damages are measured by net income.
legal_issues: Whether 'earnings lost' means net income or gross turnover/receipts
Whether a rent-liability award after business closure is earnings-related compensation
How Schedule 2 deductions interact with unusual special-damage heads
Who bears the burden of appealing the certificate of recoverable benefits
linked_authorities: Russell v Town and County Bank
Lim Poh Choo v Camden and Islington Area Health Authority

confidence.notes: Outcome and competing constructions are explicit in a reported split; ratio stated from the majority because that determines the appeal result.

enrichment.short_title: NMC penalty reasons and present fitness

statutes_considered.title: Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors Act 1997
Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors (Professional Conduct) Rules 1993

key_facts: Marie Needham, a staff nurse, admitted six charges of drug-administration and patient-care misconduct at Salisbury Health Care NHS Trust between September 1999 and January 2000.

The Professional Conduct Committee removed her from the register immediately, stating her fitness to practise remained impaired despite mitigation evidence of current competence in a learning-disabilities care home.
She appealed under section 12; the court rejected her application to withdraw earlier admissions of fact and misconduct.
The central penalty issue was whether her present ability to administer medicines safely had been adequately addressed and explained.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 12 of the Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors Act 1997 against removal from the professional register.
enrichment.outcome: Penalty quashed; full rehearing on penalty ordered before a new Professional Conduct Committee with structured reasons required.
enrichment.ratio: Fairness requires a professional conduct committee to give adequate reasons when finding present fitness to practise impaired, especially where evidence is directed to current competence; a bare conclusion without explaining why mitigation evidence was rejected is unlawful, and a structured issue-by-issue approach should be adopted so a later restoration application can be intelligently considered.
legal_issues: Whether removal from the register was excessive
Whether the committee should have tested current drug-administration knowledge
Whether adequate reasons were given for present impairment
Whether admissions of fact and misconduct could be withdrawn on appeal
linked_authorities: Brabazon-Drenning v United Kingdom Central Council

confidence.notes: Outcome announced at hearing with detailed reserved reasons; penalty quashed on inadequate reasons ground.

enrichment.short_title: Lifetime anonymity for Mary Bell and daughter
key_facts: X, formerly known as Mary Bell, was convicted in 1968 of manslaughter of two children when aged 11 and later given a new identity on release.
Her daughter Y was born in 1984, warded, and protected by injunction until majority; both sought lifetime anonymity from identification of current names and addresses.
Repeated press and public interest, prior relocations, and medical evidence showed serious risk of intrusion and harm to X's mental health if anonymity lapsed.
Major newspaper defendants and the Attorney General did not oppose injunctions in principle; orders contra mundum were sought.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court claim for final lifetime injunctions restraining disclosure of identity and whereabouts, following interim orders.
enrichment.outcome: Lifetime injunctions contra mundum granted to protect the current identities and whereabouts of X and Y, with liberty to apply to vary or discharge.
enrichment.ratio: Exceptionally, lifetime contra mundum injunctions may be granted where limited confidential information—present identity and location—is not in the public domain and Article 8 rights, including protection of mental health and family life for a rehabilitated child offender and her innocent adult daughter, outweigh Article 10 freedom of expression; the cases of released child killers remain rare and do not broaden confidentiality law generally.
legal_issues: Whether lifetime anonymity could be justified under Article 8
Whether Articles 2 or 3 required protection
Whether Y was entitled to continuing anonymity after adulthood
Compliance with section 12 Human Rights Act and balancing against press freedom
linked_authorities: Venables v News Group Newspapers Ltd
Attorney General v Guardian Newspapers Ltd (No 2)

confidence.notes: Detailed final judgment with explicit balancing exercise and order terms; exceptional-facts caveat clearly stated.

key_facts: John Mills was convicted of driving with excess alcohol after failing to provide breath at Skelmersdale police station and giving blood on 2 March 2001.
PC Cross marked the sample 'ERP 2100', but the courier later collected a differently marked specimen from the ERP fridge and the analyst's label wrongly recorded Chorley rather than Skelmersdale.
No evidence showed who placed the sample in the fridge or who completed the analyst label; the Crown Court inferred continuity without explaining its reasoning.
Mrs Slater's section 16 certificate showed 90 mg per 100 ml ten days after sampling.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Preston Crown Court upholding conviction in the magistrates' court.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; case remitted to the Crown Court with a direction to acquit.
enrichment.ratio: Section 16 of the Road Traffic Offenders Act 1988 makes an analyst's certificate conclusive proof of analysis but not of identity and continuity; where labelling and handling evidence leave a significant lacuna as to whether the analysed blood was the defendant's specimen, the prosecution has not proved its case to the criminal standard and conviction cannot stand.
legal_issues: Whether continuity of the blood specimen was proved
Effect of a section 16 analyst certificate on identity of the sample
Whether Paterson v DPP remains applicable under the 1988 legislation
Ancillary challenges to arrest, blood request, and section 78 exclusion
linked_authorities: Paterson v Director of Public Prosecutions

confidence.notes: Single decisive ground on specimen continuity; appellate court answered the stated question in the negative.

enrichment.short_title: Collecting bank indemnity for forged cheque
key_facts: Zeneca drew a crossed 'account payee only' cheque to Linklaters; a third party presented it to Banco Popular Español in Las Palmas for credit to a Puerto Rican company.
HSBC, as paying bank and collecting agent, credited BPE with the proceeds; Linklaters' money was lost and both banks settled with the payee.
HSBC claimed a complete implied indemnity and warranty from BPE; BPE argued Middle Temple Savings was wrong or distinguishable because HSBC was also the paying bank.
Gross J found both banks causatively negligent vis-à-vis Linklaters but held HSBC entitled to full indemnity from BPE.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial court trial of contribution and indemnity claims between English and Spanish banks after settling the payee's claim.
enrichment.outcome: HSBC entitled to a complete indemnity from BPE; had indemnity failed, contribution would have been assessed two-thirds BPE and one-third HSBC.
enrichment.ratio: Following Middle Temple Savings & Bank v Midland Bank, a foreign collecting bank that presents a cheque for collection impliedly indemnifies and warrants its English agent bank against liability to the true owner where the cheque is wrongly paid; that indemnity is not excluded by the agent bank's own negligence to the third party, nor by the agent also acting as paying bank, and clear banking practice supports allocating the loss to the collecting bank rather than its agent.
legal_issues: Whether Middle Temple Savings was binding and correctly decided
Whether HSBC as paying bank could claim an implied indemnity or warranty
Whether BPE's 'prior endorsements guaranteed' stamp created an express indemnity
Apportionment of contributory negligence between the banks
linked_authorities: Middle Temple Savings & Bank Ltd v Midland Bank Ltd
Marfani & Co Ltd v Midland Bank Ltd
Kai Yung v May & Baker Ltd
Dubai Aluminium Co Ltd v Salaam

confidence.notes: Long trial judgment but conclusion on indemnity following Middle Temple is explicit; contribution figures are obiter but clearly stated.
